html:
The big picture

Chapter 5's sequence types find an element by its position. This chapter adds two built-in aggregate types that find an element by its content, so they have no index at all. A dictionary (dict, also called a map or associative array) stores key-value pairs. You look a value up by its key with d[k], which only looks like indexing ("pseudo-subscripting"). A set (set, or the immutable frozenset) is a collection in the mathematical sense: no duplicates, no order, and fast membership tests. It comes with the set operations union |, intersection &, difference - and symmetric difference ^. Both types share one rule that explains most of the chapter. Keys and set elements must be immutable (strictly, hashable), because the container files each one by a value computed from its content, and that value must never change. The differences: a dict keeps the order of insertion, but the iteration order of a set is undefined. Like lists, both can be built with a comprehension ({k: v for …} and {x for …}). Python itself stores its namespaces as dictionaries, which globals(), locals() and vars() let you inspect.

Built-in data types — dictionaries and sets

Pre-defined data types with aggregate content (cont'd), many values per variable.

  • Mutable: can be changed after instantiation.
  • Immutable: cannot be changed after instantiation.
CategoryTypeMutableExample literals
Dictionary (map, key-value pairs, associative array)dictyes{"Title": "ISOP", "SWS": 2, "ECTS": 2, "Type": "VO"} {"house": "casa", "dog": "cane", "sea": "mare" } {}
Set (in the mathematical sense)setyes{2, 3, 5, 7, 9, "Apple", "Pear"}
frozensetnofrozenset({2, 3, 5, 7, 9})

Elements cannot be accessed via their place number (index) in brackets: these data types are not subscriptable (but still iterable). They do not belong to the group of sequence data types (list, tuple, str). Slide note: although dict can be »pseudo-subscripted« with a key, cf. next pages.

Intuition

A sequence answers "what is at position 3?". A dictionary answers "what belongs to "dog"?", like a real dictionary, where you look up a word, not a page number. A set answers only "is "Apple" in here?". It is a bag of distinct things with no positions. That is why neither has an index. The d["dog"] notation borrows the bracket syntax, but the thing inside the brackets is a key, not a position.

Connection

The sets here are the finite sets from 2 Elements of Sets (Analysis 1). \in, \subseteq, \cup, \cap, \setminus become in, <=, |, &, - (table on slide 229). Mutability, aliasing and "names hold references" work exactly as in 5 Sequence Types.

dict — creation

The data type dict allows mutable pairs of (possibly heterogeneous) elements of the form Key : Value:

dictionary = {"house": "casa", "dog": "cane", "sea": "mare"}

Alternatively, function dict() creates a dictionary from a list of pairs…

dictionary = dict([("house", "casa"), ("dog", "cane"), ("sea", "mare")])

…or from keyword arguments (with the keyword specifying the key):

dictionary = dict(house="casa", dog="cane", sea="mare")

Keys must be unique within a dictionary. Inserting a key twice results in overriding:

print({"house": "casa", "dog": "cane", "sea": "mare", "sea": "oceano"})
{'house': 'casa', 'dog': 'cane', 'sea': 'oceano'}

Keys must be instances of immutable data types, values can be any instances. (Slide note: to guarantee a stable organization of the data structure.)

Why must keys be immutable, when values may be anything?

A dict does not search its pairs one by one. It computes a number from the key (its hash, hash(k)) and uses that number to decide where the pair is stored. A lookup d[k] recomputes hash(k) and goes straight to that place, so the time does not grow with the size of the dictionary. If a key could change after insertion (say a list that gets an element appended), its hash would change too, and the pair would sit in the wrong place, where no lookup ever finds it. Immutable keys (int, str, tuple of immutables, frozenset) cannot change, so their hash is stable. Values are never hashed, so they may be mutable. Trying {[1, 2]: 1} raises TypeError: … unhashable type: 'list', while {(1, 2): "ok"} works. The same reasoning explains why set elements must be immutable (slide 228).

Intuition

"Keys are unique" is what makes d[k] well defined: one key, one value. A second "sea": … is therefore not a second entry. It is an assignment to the existing key, and the later value wins, just as x = 1; x = 2 leaves x == 2.

dict — usage

Retrieving the value for a given key using the index operator [] (»associative array«):

print(dictionary["house"])        # 'casa'

Iterating over the keys of a dictionary:

for key in dictionary:
    print(key, end=" ")           # house dog sea

Iterating over the values of a dictionary:

for value in dictionary.values():
    print(value, end=" ")         # casa cane mare

Iterating over the key/value pairs of a dictionary:

for pair in dictionary.items():
    print(pair, end=" ")          # ('house', 'casa') ('dog', 'cane') ('sea', 'mare')

for key, value in dictionary.items():
    print(key, "➝", value, end=" ")   # house ➝ casa dog ➝ cane sea ➝ mare

Slide note: the iteration follows the order of insertion.

Intuition

for key, value in dictionary.items() is the tuple unpacking from 5 Sequence Types. Each element of items() is a 2-tuple (key, value), and the loop variables key, value unpack it on every pass, just as a, b = ("house", "casa") would. The plain for key in dictionary gives only the keys because that is what iterating over a dictionary is defined to produce.

Common mistake

Wrong idea: "I can tidy a dictionary by deleting entries inside for k in d:." Why it fails: changing the size of a dictionary while iterating over it raises RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration. This is the dictionary version of the "changing the iteration object" trap in 5 Sequence Types. Right model: iterate over a snapshot of the keys (for k in list(d):) and delete from d, or build a new dictionary with a comprehension (slide 227).

dict — operations

Specific operations (d, d1, d2 denote dictionaries, k a key):

NotationMeaning
len(d)Number of pairs in d
d[k]Access to value with key k. Reading: yields the value associated with k or KeyError if k does not exist. Writing: defines or changes the value associated with k.
del d[k]Deletes key k and its value
k in dTrue if d contains k
k not in dTrue if d does not contain k
d1 | d2Combines the two dictionaries d1 and d2 (also: d1 |= d2)
d.items()Returns an iterable object covering all (key, value) pairs
d.keys()Returns an iterable object covering all keys
d.values()Returns an iterable object covering all values

Specific operations (d, d1, d2 denote dictionaries, k a key, seq an instance of a sequence type, x an arbitrary instance):

NotationMeaning
d.clear()Empties (but does not delete) d
d.copy()Ceates a copy of d
d.get(k[, x])d[k], if d contains k, otherwise x, if present, otherwise None
d.setdefault(k[, x])d[k] = x (or None, if x is not present) if d does not contain k
d.pop(k)Returns d[k] and deletes the entry k
d.popitem()Returns an arbitrary key/value pair and deletes it from d
d1.update(d2)d1 |= d2
dict.fromkeys(seq[, x])Returns a new dictionary with keys taken from seq and all values equal to x (or None, if x is not given)

(Square brackets in the notation column mark an optional argument, as in the Python documentation: d.get(k) or d.get(k, x).)

Unclear (slides 222 and 229)

"Ceates a copy" is a typo for "Creates a copy" (the same typo appears on both slides; it is transcribed as printed).

Unclear (slide 222)

d.popitem() is described as removing an "arbitrary" pair. Since Python 3.7 the order is guaranteed: popitem() removes and returns the pair inserted last (LIFO). Example: after d.setdefault("cat", "gatto") on the house/dog/sea dictionary, d.popitem() returns ('cat', 'gatto'). "Arbitrary" is still safe advice if you don't want your code to depend on the order. It is unclear whether the lecture means "don't rely on which pair" or describes older Python versions.

Why do get and setdefault exist, when d[k] already reads and writes?

d[k] raises KeyError for a missing key, so every lookup of a possibly-missing key would need an if k in d: first. d.get(k, x) folds that test into one call and returns the fallback x instead of failing (d.get("cat") ➝ None, d.get("cat", "?") ➝ '?'). It never changes d. d.setdefault(k, x) goes one step further. It inserts k: x only if k is missing, and in both cases it also returns d[k] (the slide's table leaves out the return value). So d.setdefault("cat", "gatto") returns 'gatto' and leaves the pair in d. For a key that is already there, nothing changes and the existing value is returned.

Common mistake

Wrong idea: "In d1 | d2, a key that occurs in both keeps the value from d1" (or: "Python raises an error for duplicate keys"). Why it fails: | works like the duplicate-key rule on slide 219: the pairs of d2 are inserted after those of d1, so the right-hand value wins. {"a": 1, "b": 2} | {"b": 3, "c": 4} ➝ {'a': 1, 'b': 3, 'c': 4}. Right model: d1 | d2 makes a new dictionary. d1 |= d2 and d1.update(d2) change d1 in place, also with d2 winning. (| for dictionaries needs Python 3.9 or newer.)

Common mistake

Wrong idea: "d.copy() gives me a completely independent dictionary." Why it fails: like l[:] for lists (5 Sequence Types), copy() is shallow. The new dictionary has its own pairs, but each value is the same object. With a = {"x": [1]}; b = a.copy(); b["x"].append(2), a is now {'x': [1, 2]} too. And plain b = a does not copy at all: it is a second name for the same dictionary (aliasing). Right model: copy() protects against adding, removing or re-assigning keys in the copy, not against mutating a shared mutable value.

dict — example: counting characters

Riddle on the slide: extend the program to draw a histogram by defining and calling a function def histogram (data:dict[str, int]) -> None:.

The histogram the riddle asks for: one bar per character of the first input text, bar height = number of occurrences (window titled "Characters").

Let us use a dictionary to count how often each character occurs in a string:

while (text := input("Your text: ")) != "":
    counter: dict[str, int] = { } # Create an empty dictionary
    for c in text:
        if c in counter:       # Character c has already been seen
            counter[c] += 1    # One more occurrence found
        else:                  # First occurrence found - insert
            counter[c] = 1
    print(counter)
Your text: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
{'I': 1, 'n': 6, ' ': 16, 't': 5, 'h': 5, 'e': 5, 'b': 1, 'g': 2, 'i': 3, 'w': 4, 'a': 5, 's': 3, 'W': 3, 'o': 5, 'r': 3, 'd': 7, ',': 2, 'G': 2, '.': 1}
Your text: In the beginning the Universe was created. This has made a lot of people very angry and been widely regarded as a bad move.
{'I': 1, 'n': 8, ' ': 23, 't': 4, 'h': 4, 'e': 17, 'b': 3, 'g': 4, 'i': 5, 'U': 1, 'v': 3, 'r': 6, 's': 5, 'w': 2, 'a': 11, 'c': 1, 'd': 7, '.': 2, 'T': 1, 'm': 2, 'l': 3, 'o': 4, 'f': 1, 'p': 2, 'y': 3}
Your text:
Intuition

The dictionary is a row of tally sheets, one per character, created the moment a character is first seen. if c in counter asks "is there already a sheet for c?". If yes, add a stroke (+= 1). If no, start a new sheet with one stroke (= 1). The if is needed because counter[c] += 1 means counter[c] = counter[c] + 1, and reading counter[c] for a new c would raise KeyError. The same loop in one line uses get: counter[c] = counter.get(c, 0) + 1. The output lists the characters in the order they first appeared (order of insertion).

Worked example — grouping with a dictionary (count → collect)

Task: group the words ["robot", "arm", "sensor", "motor", "AI", "gear"] by their length.

  1. Choose key and value: key = word length (int, immutable ✓), value = list of the words with that length.
  2. Create an empty dictionary: by_len: dict[int, list[str]] = {}.
  3. For each word, ensure the key exists, then add: by_len.setdefault(len(w), []).append(w). For a new length this inserts [] and returns it, and for a known length it returns the existing list. Either way .append(w) adds the word to the list stored in the dictionary.
  4. Result: {5: ['robot', 'motor'], 3: ['arm'], 6: ['sensor'], 2: ['AI'], 4: ['gear']}. The keys appear in the order of their first occurrence. This is the counter pattern with "add one" replaced by "append". It is the same idea, a dictionary of accumulators.

dict — example variant: case insensitive, sorted output

while (text := input("Your text: ")) != "":
    counter: dict[str, int] = { }
    for c in text.upper():         # Convert letters to upper case
        if c in counter:
            counter[c] += 1
        else:
            counter[c] = 1

    l = list(counter.keys())      # List of all letters ...
    l.sort()                      # ... is sorted ...
    for k in l:                   # ... and iterated over
        print(f"{k}: {counter[k]}")
Your text: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.

,: 2

A: 5
B: 1
D: 7
E: 5
G: 4
H: 5
I: 4
N: 6
O: 5
R: 3
S: 3
T: 5
W: 7
Your text:
Why does the program first copy the keys into a list before sorting?

A dictionary has no sort() method: its order is the order of insertion, and you cannot rearrange it. counter.keys() is a view of the keys, not a list, so it has no sort() either. list(counter.keys()) makes a real list, l.sort() sorts it in place (characters by their code: the space, , and . come before the capital letters), and the loop then looks every key up in counter. Upper-casing first merges w/W, g/G and i/I, which is why W: 7 = 4 + 3 and G: 4 = 2 + 2 here. (sorted(counter) would do the copy and the sort in one step.)

dict — examples: some Python system dictionaries

Python maintains a lot of its runtime information in dictionaries that can be inspected.

1) globals() — the global namespace dictionary

globals() returns a dictionary containing all names defined at the top level of the current module. It includes

  • functions
  • classes
  • global variables
  • imported modules
x = 10
def f(): pass

print(globals().keys())
print(globals()["x"])
print(type(globals()["x"]))
print(globals()["f"])
print(type(globals()["f"]))
{'__name__': '__main__', '__doc__': None, '__package__': None, '__loader__': <_frozen_importlib_external.SourceFileLoader object at 0x102a1de00>, '__spec__': None, '__annotations__': {}, '__builtins__': <module 'builtins' (built-in)>, '__file__': '/Users/mhitz/ISOP.py/Programs/VO.py', '__cached__': None, 'x': 10, 'f': <function f at 0x102b732e0>}
10
<class 'int'>
<function f at 0x100f632e0>
<class 'function'>

(On the slide the keys of the output are coloured for readability.)

Unclear (slide 225)

The first output line does not match print(globals().keys()). It shows the whole dictionary with keys and values, which is what print(globals()) prints. print(globals().keys()) prints only the names, in the form dict_keys(['__name__', '__doc__', …, 'x', 'f']). The two addresses of f also differ (0x102b732e0 vs. 0x100f632e0), so the output box seems to combine two different runs. The point of the slide is unaffected: x and f are ordinary entries of the global namespace dictionary.

Intuition

A namespace is the table Python consults to turn a name into an object, and it really is a dict, with the variable names as keys and the referenced objects as values. x = 10 at the top level effectively does globals()["x"] = 10. Reading x looks up globals()["x"], and a NameError is the namespace's version of a KeyError. This is the memory model of 3 Variables, Data Types and Expressions (names hold references) made visible.

2) locals() — the local namespace dictionary

locals() returns a dictionary of names in the current scope. Inside a function it

  • contains parameter names
  • local variables
  • function-level definitions
def g (a, b):
    c = a + b
    print(locals())

g(10, 3.14)
{'a': 10, 'b': 3.14, 'c': 13.14}

3) vars() — generic, returns the __dict__ of an object

vars(obj) returns the object's attribute dictionary, i.e., obj.__dict__, while vars() is the same as globals():

# Somewhere in the UBO program:
print(vars(UBO.universe()[0]))
{'_UBO__r': 0.05, '_UBO__pos': (-0.5687599392861821, 0.5751400507688036), '_UBO__v': (0.004182058377104274, -0.015976112521355647), '_UBO__color': 'red'}
Unclear (slide 226)

"vars() is the same as globals()" holds only at the top level of a module. In general, vars() without an argument returns the local namespace, i.e. it behaves like locals(). Called inside g above, it would give {'a': 10, 'b': 3.14, 'c': 13.14}, not the global names. At the top level, local and global namespace are the same dictionary, which is presumably the case the slide means.

Connection

The UBO output is the bouncing-ball class from 7 Classes and Objects. Each object keeps its instance variables in its own dictionary __dict__, with the attribute names as keys. The names show name mangling: a private attribute __r defined in class UBO is stored as _UBO__r. That is how the double underscore keeps the attribute "private". It is renamed, not hidden.

dict — dictionary comprehension

Dictionary comprehension works like list comprehension: we just use a key-value expression k:v to construct the dictionary.

Examples: create a dictionary mapping numbers to their squares for the numbers from 1 to 5:

squares = {k: k**2              # key-value expression
           for k in range(1, 6)}  # loop clause
print(squares)
{1: 1, 2: 4, 3: 9, 4: 16, 5: 25}

Suppose you have a dictionary of student names and their scores, and you want a new dictionary with only students who passed (score ≥ 50):

scores = {"Alice": 85, "Bob": 42,
          "Clara": 77, "David": 48}
passed = {name: score
          for name, score in scores.items()
          if score >= 50}          # filter clause or conditional clause
print(passed)
{'Alice': 85, 'Clara': 77}
Worked example — from loop to dictionary comprehension (inverting a dictionary)

Task: turn {"house": "casa", "dog": "cane"} (English → Italian) into Italian → English.

  1. Write the loop on foot: inv = {} then for k, v in d.items(): inv[v] = k.
  2. Move the assignment to the front as key: value: what is written into inv is the pair v: k.
  3. Append the loop clause unchanged: inv = {v: k for k, v in d.items()}.
  4. Check: {'casa': 'house', 'cane': 'dog'} ✓.
  5. Check the key rule: the old values become the new keys, so they must be immutable and distinct. If two words had the same translation, the later one would overwrite the earlier (slide 219).

set and frozenset — creation

The iterable data types set and frozenset allow mutable and immutable sets of (possibly heterogeneous) immutable elements (to guarantee a stable organization of the data structure):

long_months = { 1, 3, 5, 7, 8, 10, 12 }     # Creates a set
empty = { } # Not an empty set, but an empty dict!

Alternatively, functions set() and frozenset() create (frozen) sets from iterable objects:

even_under10 = set(range(0, 10, 2))       # ➝ {0, 2, 4, 6, 8}
empty = frozenset()                       # ➝ empty frozen set
q1 = frozenset(["Jan", "Feb", "Mar"])     # Create frozenset from list

Similar to list comprehension, set comprehension can be used to create set objects:

even_under10 = {x for x in range(0, 10, 2)} # { 2k | k∈ℕ, 0 ≤ 2k < 10}
even_under10 = {x for x in range(10) if x % 2 == 0}
print({x*x for x in range(10)})             # Print first 10 squares
{0, 1, 64, 4, 36, 9, 16, 49, 81, 25}

Slide note: the sequence of elements is undefined and can change even between program runs.

Unclear (slide 228)

The comment \{2k \mid k \in \mathbb{N},\ 0 \le 2k < 10\} describes \{0, 2, 4, 6, 8\} only if 0 \in \mathbb{N}. Under the convention \mathbb{N} = \{1, 2, 3, \dots\} (common in analysis courses) the 0 would be missing. k \in \mathbb{N}_0 is the unambiguous form.

Common mistake

Wrong idea: "{} is the empty set, since sets are written with braces." Why it fails: the braces were given to dictionaries first, so {} is an empty dict: type({}) ➝ <class 'dict'>. Python tells the two literals apart by their content. {1} is a set, and {1: 2} is a dict. Right model: the empty set is set() (and frozenset()). A program that starts with s = {} and later calls s.add(x) fails with AttributeError: 'dict' object has no attribute 'add'.

Why does a set print its elements in a "random" order, and why do duplicates vanish?

A set is filed by hash, exactly like dictionary keys (see the Why on slide 219). Each element goes to a place determined by hash(x), and printing walks through those places, not through the order you wrote the elements in. For small ints the hash is the number itself, which is why the squares come out in a scrambled but repeatable pattern. For strings the hash is randomised every time Python starts, so the order of a set of strings can differ between program runs. A second copy of an element has the same hash and compares equal, so it lands on the place that is already taken and is simply not added again. That is how set(workshop_python) on slide 230 removes the duplicate names.

set and frozenset — operations

s, t denote (frozen) sets, x an element. Slide note: in the alternatives (method forms), t may be of an arbitrary sequence type.

NotationAlternativeMeaning
len(s)\lvert s \rvert
x [not] in s[\neg]\,(x \in s)
s <= ts.issubset(t)s \subseteq t
s < ts \subset t
s >= ts.issuperset(t)s \supseteq t
s > ts \supset t
s | ts.union(t)s \cup t (analogous: s |= t)
s & ts.intersection(t)s \cap t (analogous: s &= t)
s - ts.difference(t)s \setminus t (analogous: s -= t)
s ^ ts.symmetric_difference(t)Symmetric difference, (s \cup t) \setminus (s \cap t) (analogous: s ^= t)
s.isdisjoint(t)s \cap t = \emptyset
s.copy()Ceates a copy of s

Slide note: in the case of frozenset, these operators (|=, &=, -=, ^=) create and assign a new instance to s.

Intuition

s < t is the proper subset: s \subseteq t and s \ne t. So {1, 2} < {1, 2} is False, while {1, 2} <= {1, 2} is True. The symmetric difference s ^ t is "in exactly one of the two": everything in the union except what both share (the set version of exclusive or). The frozenset note is the +=-on-a-string story from 5 Sequence Types again. An immutable object cannot change, so fs |= {3} builds a new frozenset and rebinds the name fs to it, and any other name for the old object still sees the old set.

Common mistake

Wrong idea: "s | t and s.union(t) are interchangeable in every case." Why it fails: the operators need sets on both sides: {1, 2, 3} | [3, 4] raises TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for |: 'set' and 'list'. The methods accept any iterable for t (that is the slide note): {1, 2, 3}.union([3, 4]) ➝ {1, 2, 3, 4}. Right model: convert first (s | set(t)) or use the method form whenever t is a list, tuple, string or range.

set and frozenset — example

Given are the lists of students registered for two different workshops:

  • workshop_python = ["Anna", "Ben", "Clara", "Ben", "Dina", "Anna"]
  • workshop_data = ["Clara", "Ella", "Ben", "Felix", "Anna", "Ella"]

Determine

  • all students who attend both workshops,
  • all students who attend at least one workshop,
  • all students who attend only the Python workshop.
# 1) Convert to sets
python = set(workshop_python)
data = set(workshop_data)

# 2) Set operations
both = python & data              # ∩
anyone = python | data            # ∪
only_python = python - data       # \

print("Both workshops:", both)
print("At least one:", anyone)
print("Only Python:", only_python)
Both workshops: {'Anna', 'Clara', 'Ben'}
At least one: {'Dina', 'Clara', 'Ben', 'Ella', 'Felix', 'Anna'}
Only Python: {'Dina'}
Worked example — translating a question into set operations

Task: known = {"Python", "C", "Rust"} and a job ad lists wanted = ["C", "Java", "C", "Python"].

  1. Make both sides sets (and drop duplicates): w = set(wanted) ➝ {'C', 'Java', 'Python'}.
  2. "Which wanted languages do I know?" = in both: known & w ➝ {'C', 'Python'}.
  3. "Which do I know that nobody asked for?" = in known but not in w: known - w ➝ {'Rust'}.
  4. "In exactly one of the two lists?" = symmetric difference: known ^ w ➝ {'Java', 'Rust'}.
  5. "Any overlap at all?": known.isdisjoint(wanted) ➝ False (the method takes the list directly). Recipe: phrase the question as "in A and/or/but not B", then pick &, |, - or ^. Don't rely on the printed order; sort (sorted(...)) if the output must be stable.

set and frozenset — iteration

The behaviour of the loop for e in s: where s is of type set is not deterministic in terms of the order in which elements are iterated over, since sets in Python are unordered.

When we iterate over a set, the iteration order depends on the internal storage mechanism, which can vary between

  • Python versions, and even
  • different executions of the same program.

However, iteration is deterministic within the same execution: in a single execution, the order of iteration over a set is deterministic as long as the set is not modified during iteration.

Common mistake

Wrong idea: "Sets and dictionaries are both 'unordered', so neither has a reliable order." Why it fails: since Python 3.7 a dict is guaranteed to keep the order of insertion (slide 220). A set gives no such guarantee (slides 228, 231). Code that prints a set and compares the text with an expected answer can pass on one run and fail on the next. Right model: need order → use a dict or a list, or sorted(s) when you output a set. Need only membership/uniqueness → a set is fine.

set — operations for mutable sets

Specific operations for mutable sets (s denotes a set, t an arbitrary sequence type, x an element):

NotationMeaning
s.clear()Empties (but does not delete) s
s.add(x)Inserts x into s
s.update(t)s |= t
s.difference_update(t)s -= t
s.intersection_update(t)s &= t
s.symmetric_difference_update(t)s ^= t
s.discard(x)s -= { x }
s.remove(x)Deletes x in s. Yields an error, if x not in s
s.pop()Returns an arbitrary element \in s and deletes it. Yields an error, if s = \emptyset
Intuition

discard and remove both delete an element. The difference is what happens when it isn't there: discard silently does nothing (like s -= {x}), while remove raises KeyError. Use remove when a missing element would mean a bug you want to hear about, and discard when "make sure it's gone" is all you need. It is the same split as d.get(k) vs. d[k] for dictionaries. These mutating methods exist only for set. A frozenset has none of them, because it cannot change.
